Oh boy! My first review and it's on Rainworld! Playing video games has made me kinda brain-dead because of how simple the formulas have gotten, but this game completely flipped me. A surprisingly weak protagonist, no shops, no upgrades, almost no dialogue or tutorials, no health or stamina bars. The game just plops you in the middle of Outskirts and says "explore". For anyone interested in this game, expect Rainworld to minimally reward you for your actions and heavily punish any mistakes. It's running completely off the hope that players will be mystified by the world and will push through all the deaths just to see what the next area reveals and what creatures inhabit it. Admittedly, this game is demanding a lot out of it's players and, as a result, many are discouraged from actually completing it, which is unfortunate since what lies underneath is a thrilling, beautiful, and melancholic depiction of what it feels like to be a pathetic creature in a mysteriously hostile world.
Rainworld isn't my favorite game (not that I have one), but it's without a doubt the most unique game I've ever played and I look forward to whatever Videocult may have in store for the future.

This is a beautiful, fascinating game. I don't buy this idea that it's too difficult - if it's hard then that's part of the learning process, learning to survive as a slugcat. Yes the controls may be a little awkward, but again that's part of the learning process. If all you want is instant gratification then maybe this isn't for you but if you want something deeper and are prepared to put in the time and energy then this is a brlliant game. And some of the best artwork I've seen in ages. I could probably do without the timed fatal rain episodes but having that hanging over you adds to the sense of danger and adds to the atmosphere.

After almost 400 hours of playtime and nearly 100% achievement completion, I would easily consider Rain World one of the very best gaming experiences I've ever been through. I love this game, and I really wish more people knew about it.

No, it's not easy. Often annoying or frustrating.

But the art, the world and creature design? All of it is just... outstanding, and I could get lost in its map for hours. Some things will always be frustrating, but the more of the vast world and its creatures you experience, the more you can adapt and overcome the challenges you face. It doesn't pull its punches, but that just makes progressing and delving into the game's secrets even more satisfying.

Plus, you get to play as an adorable slugcat! What's not to like?

I got interested in this game because it really reminded me of the grim, dark artwork from the artist: Zdzislaw Beksinski. So far that holds true.

Other than that, at first it is very difficult to understand the controls, but once you get used to it, it becomes very fun to explore the areas and see new creatures. If you're a fan of Hollow Knight, or games like that, you'd probably like this.

The controls take some getting used to, but once you git gud you are rewarded with intense action, incredible environmental story telling and a deeply immersive atmosphere.
I spent hours just sitting still and observing how different lifeforms interact with each other.
There are so many breathtaking and hair-raising moments along the player's journey, my favourite being the mindbending build-up and pay-off in the Iterator "Five Pebbles" .

If you're the type of person who doesn't mind wandering around aimlessly without the game ever giving you a direction, then this might be for you. Not saying this as something necessarily negative but it just isn't my cup of tea.

Possibly one of the most cryptic and obnoxious survival games I've ever played. Chock-full of obscure and trivial mechanics, totally random "progress" and no real direction or understanding of what you should be doing or why other than simply making it to the next day, unique yet totally garbage controls and physics that cause you to constantly do things by accident (or not at all) only to support the game's aesthetic at the cost of functional, fun gameplay, an extremely irritating and useless "guide" entity that never gives you the information you need when you actually need it, and a needlessly complicated map that serves only to get you killed.

I like survival games, I'm even good at them, and I've wanted to play this game for all the years it was in development, but it has all the annoyance of one and yet none of the satisfying gameplay or mechanics. I like the art, graphics, and setting, but mechanically it's really irritating and contrived for the sake of seeming like it has any depth when it's actually painfully simple; it's just a game that makes every effort to stop you from actually having fun.

A beautiful and difficult game with excellent platforming and environments to explore. The movement system is quite tight and feels really nice to do, though many things are difficult at first. The way the creatures of Rain world move is organic and interesting, even funny to watch at times. Map wise it's pretty expansive with wonderful scenery and great level design.

The sound design fits like a glove and the music is fantastic! The threat themes in this game are very cool with irregular beats so they don't get tiring even after they play for a while, which it will because every pixel in the game wants you dead.
The environmental sounds can either be quite soothing or conjure up something truly intimidating.
There is lore in this game but you have to work to get to it and it's incredibly interesting.

Rain World feels like it wants to be both a platformer and a survival game and it fails at both.

The controls are clunky and often feel inconsistent, especially in regards to horizonal climbing or moving though tight spaces, the latter being something you can expect to do a lot of. The hunger and karma systems, while successful in adding a survival element to the game in the form of gathering food, mainly just serve to add a layer of tedium to saving/checkpoints and moving between areas. The ecosystem, while technically impressive, adds a random factor to enemy locations that leads to a constant chance for any path to be arbitrarily blocked off for any given cycle.

5 hours in and it looks like a major character is permenantly injured because I ate the wrong food in an area where food was sparse to begin with, so I think I'll just leave it here. Despite being a fan of games typically considered hard, I find myself with less and less patience for "bad on purpose" type game design. Really feels like the game should either be much shorter per playthrough, or commit more fully to it's platforming or survival sides instead of fumbling both.

Feedback:
Improve the in-game minimap, don't use a layered parallax scrolling layout, just go for simple 2d with smooth zooming, or at least pause the game when viewing the minimap. Right now it's very chaotic, results in googling jpegs.

Storytelling needs a lot of work here, here it is in a partial state of very slow lore-discovery after 2/3 of the game, with no incentive for the player, all the work done on the rich lore is wasted this way.

Player character should have more interactions with the ever-dominant environment, build the character up a little, not just through random and sparse (albeit fancy) artwork. At least a little bit of monologue here and there.

Pearl lore should be presented or at least unlocked upon finding them, not having to bring each of them to one spot in the huge world, especially since the maximum you can carry is 3.

Rain World is the most unique game I have ever played. It constructs difficulty from intentional jank and unfairness. The slugcat’s controls are unintuitive and wonky. You really feel like a freak of nature struggling to survive in a broken ecosystem. There are no predictable enemy patterns to learn, but rather creatures with motives to exploit. Mechanical skill won’t do nearly as much for you as careful observation, situational awareness, and resourcefulness. And even then, you’re going to die a lot. The task of merely surviving feels sisyphean; theme expressed via gameplay mechanics. The world feels alien and strange, unknowable. Heinous creatures, inexplicable technology, the entire world drenched in torrents of rain so severe they kill everything not tucked away in a den. The soundtrack contributes excellently to this unfamiliarity. It remains one of the most impactful gaming experiences I’ve had, and I’m sure I’ll continue to think about it for years.

I could spend hours writing this review, but I'll keep it brief. I've played games all my life. Of the titles released in the last decade which I've finished, Rain World is the best. It is very difficult and requires extreme patience. It completely lacks numerical motivators and instant gratification, is harshly punishing, and random elements can significantly alter the challenge level without the player's input. I wouldn't have it any other way, though, as it is precisely because of those things that Rain World is the most consistently immersive video game experience of any I have had. If you think you can embrace the mechanics' uncomfortable nature, especially if you like minimalist, experience-oriented games such as Ico or Shadow of the Colossus, then play Rain World. It won't be for everyone, but for some, it will be an unforgettable treasure.

This game changed my view on death and ultimately my view on my own suicidal thoughts and tendencies. The way it handles death, with the aspect of trying and trying again, really emphasizes the message of not giving up quite yet; that every challenge is surmountable. The way the long-forgotten race of the game eagerly sought out death, with one of the characters being frustratingly obsessed with it, reminded me much of myself throughout my life.

You play as a small animal in an alien ecosystem known as a "Slugcat", where you must survive day to day (or cycle to cycle) as a creature on the lower rungs of the food chain. Left without a goal, the path you forge is up to your own devices. Will you end the cycle of life you're contained in, or can you seek out something more?

Easy way to describe what this game is:

The adventure of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
2d exploration of Super Metroid
Sheer difficulty and frustration of Getting Over it

If you like all of these 3 games combined, you'll like it a lot.

I've heard it said that insanity is doing the same thing repetedly and expecting different results. If that's the case, then this game is designed to encourage insanity.

You may die dozens of times at some points. Often you won't be able to tell what you did wrong. Sometimes an important mechanic isn't explained to you. Sometimes weird jumping physics will kill you. Sometimes enemies will instakill you as you enter a room. Sometimes enemies will camp the only exit to a path, and the timer will kill you. Sometimes you can't find the safe room, and the timer will kill you. Sometimes randomly placed invisible ranged enemies will kill you.

And during these times, you may find yourself doing the same thing, dieing over and over, because you're not sure what you're doing wrong. And then, seemingly at random, you'll succeed. But you didn't do anything different, the game just seemed to cooperate this time.

Congratulations, you're insane now.

... But if you'd rather not be as insane as me, you could probably just watch someone play the game on youtube with all the tedium edited out. I mean, I guess.

This game is so unique that I'm not even sure how to review it, but I'm going to try. It's a game that guards its secrets very well, and frankly doesn't give you very much incentive to seek them out. You need to have a self-driven sense of curiosity and some real determination to get anywhere with it, which is why so many people end up quitting before they get very far. That being said, it has some extremely cool moments and deep lore if you're patient enough to reach them. It took me a few tries to get into it, but I really wanted to find out why it's such a cult classic, and now I can FINALLY say that I understand.

tldr.text: Very Positive (94%): players praise the story, the challenge, and the art.
The gameplay and combat draw the most complaints, ahead of difficulty and the story.

details.text: Recent reviews are about as positive as the all-time score, and complaints about gameplay and combat are less common now.
Players with under 2 hours are 64% positive, while those with over 50 hours are 99% positive, so the early hours may not win over some new players.
